Read the file — 34 lines, a `Cache` type plus a `LoadNames` reader. Tracing each function for defects now.

- `LoadNames`: no `Close`, single `Read` into a fixed 4096 buffer, error discarded.
- `Cache`: `Add` takes no lock while `Count` does; no constructor initializes `names`.

Six findings under the bugs lens:

**Critical**
1. `Add` mutates `c.names` without holding `c.mu` while `Count` reads under it — concurrent use is a data race and the Go runtime's map race detector throws `concurrent map read and map write`, crashing the process.
2. `c.names` is never allocated — the package exports no constructor, so `(&Cache{}).Add("x")` panics with `assignment to entry in nil map`.

**Major**

3. `f` is never closed — every `LoadNames` call leaks a descriptor until GC finalizes it; a loop over many files hits `EMFILE`.
4. A single `Read` of a 4096-byte buffer silently truncates any larger file, and even under 4096 bytes `Read` is permitted to return a short count. Use `os.ReadFile`.
5. `n, _ := f.Read(buf)` discards the error, so a read failure returns an empty slice and a `nil` error — indistinguishable from an empty file.

**Minor**

6. `strings.Split` on empty or newline-terminated content yields a spurious trailing `""` element.

findings.title: Add mutates the map without holding the mutex Count reads under
findings.body: Cache carries a sync.Mutex and Count locks it around the map read, but Add writes c.names[name]++ with no lock at all. The mutex therefore protects nothing: one goroutine calling Add while another calls Add or Count is an unsynchronized concurrent map access. Go's runtime map implementation detects this and throws "concurrent map writes" or "concurrent map read and map write", which is a fatal error that no recover can catch — the whole process dies. Failure case: two goroutines each call c.Add("x") on a shared *Cache; under the race detector this reports a data race immediately, and in production it either corrupts the map's internal buckets or aborts the process. That a mutex is present and used in exactly one of the two methods makes this an omission rather than a deliberate lock-free design.
findings.fix: Lock in Add the same way Count does: c.mu.Lock(); defer c.mu.Unlock() as the first line of Add.

findings.title: names map is never initialized, so Add panics on a zero-value Cache
findings.body: Cache.names is a map[string]int that nothing in the file ever allocates — there is no New/NewCache constructor and no lazy make() in Add. A map's zero value is nil, and writing to a nil map panics with "assignment to entry in nil map". Failure case: c := &Cache{}; c.Add("x") panics on line 26. Because names is unexported, a caller outside the package cannot even work around it with a composite literal — &Cache{names: map[string]int{}} does not compile from another package, so there is no way to construct a usable Cache at all. Count survives only by accident: reads from a nil map return the zero value.
findings.fix: Add a constructor that allocates the map — func New() *Cache { return &Cache{names: map[string]int{}} } — or make Add allocate lazily under the lock: if c.names == nil { c.names = map[string]int{} }.

findings.title: File descriptor leaked on every LoadNames call
findings.body: os.Open succeeds and returns f, but no path out of the function closes it — there is no defer f.Close() and no explicit close before the return on line 22. The descriptor stays open until the GC runs os.File's finalizer, which is nondeterministic and may never happen in a short-lived or low-allocation process. Failure case: a caller looping LoadNames over a directory of a few thousand files exhausts the per-process descriptor limit and every subsequent os.Open fails with "too many open files", which surfaces as a read error in unrelated code far from this function. The error return path on line 18 is fine (f is not valid there); only the success path leaks.
findings.fix: Add defer f.Close() immediately after the error check on line 19.

findings.title: Single 4096-byte Read silently truncates larger files
findings.body: The function allocates a fixed 4096-byte buffer and performs exactly one f.Read, then treats buf[:n] as the entire file contents. io.Reader makes no guarantee of filling the buffer: Read returns whatever is available, up to len(buf). Failure case: a names file of 10KB returns only the names in the first 4096 bytes, and the split of a mid-name boundary yields a corrupted final entry — with a nil error, so the caller has no signal that anything was dropped. Even for a file well under 4096 bytes, a single Read on a pipe, a slow filesystem, or an interrupted syscall may return a short count, producing a partial result. The function's name and signature promise all names in the file.
findings.fix: Replace the whole open/read sequence with data, err := os.ReadFile(path), which reads to EOF and closes the file, resolving this alongside the descriptor leak.

findings.title: Read error discarded, so a failed read is reported as an empty file
findings.body: n, _ := f.Read(buf) throws away the error. When Read fails — a bad descriptor, an I/O error, a directory passed as path (os.Open succeeds on a directory; the subsequent Read fails with EISDIR on Linux) — n is 0 and the function returns strings.Split("", "\n"), which is []string{""}, together with a nil error. Failure case: LoadNames("/some/dir") returns a one-element slice and no error; the caller cannot distinguish a genuine I/O failure from a legitimately empty file and proceeds on data it never actually read. The function already has an error return in its signature and uses it on line 18, so the failure is a swallowed error rather than a missing channel to report it.
findings.fix: Capture and check the error: n, err := f.Read(buf); if err != nil && err != io.EOF { return nil, err }. Switching to os.ReadFile removes the issue entirely.

findings.title: strings.Split yields a spurious trailing empty name
findings.body: strings.Split on a newline-terminated file produces a final empty element, and on empty content returns []string{""} rather than an empty slice. Failure case: a file containing "alice\nbob\n" — the normal shape for a text file, since editors terminate the last line — returns []string{"alice", "bob", ""}. A caller feeding that into Cache.Add records a count under the empty-string key, and a caller reporting len() sees 3 names where there are 2. An empty file yields a slice of length 1 rather than 0, so a len(names) == 0 emptiness check never fires.
findings.fix: Trim before splitting and special-case empty content, or use bufio.Scanner over the file, which skips the trailing newline and yields no line for empty input.
